I have farmed this land in Quzhou County for 45 years, and I know every corner of my 10.1 mu. The soil here is alluvial loam — decent fertility but it needs feeding if you want to fill a grain sack. My well gives good water, so irrigation is not my main worry; my main worry is balancing the cost of inputs against what I can sell at harvest. With just my wife and me in the household, labor is tight during peak times, but 10.1 mu is manageable if I plan it right.

This year I am keeping 7 mu in the wheat-maize double-cropping system and 3.1 mu in cotton. I am not changing this layout because it has worked for me, and I watched the Liu family three plots over try to shift everything to maize last year and they had trouble finding buyers for such a big single-crop volume. For the winter wheat on those 7 mu, I will plant an improved short-stalk variety that handled last winter's cold snap well. I will apply 28 kg of nitrogen per mu, 10 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium. I know 28 kg of nitrogen is on the generous side, but on my land, dropping below 25 kg always costs me at least 50 kg of grain, and at current wheat prices that loss is worse than the extra fertilizer cost. I will rotary till before sowing. I will irrigate four times from my well: the winter water around the New Year to protect from freeze, then at jointing in March, at heading in late April, and once during grain filling in mid-May. I will spray twice for weeds and one fungus/aphid pass, so two pesticide applications total. If the weather holds, I expect 500 kg per mu.

For the summer maize that follows immediately after wheat harvest, I will use a hybrid variety and plant 2.5 kg of seed per mu with no-tillage direct seeding — there is no time to waste between harvest and the next sowing if I want the maize to mature before autumn cold. Fertilizer will be 20 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times: once at sowing if the soil is dry, again at the jointing stage, and a third time at tasseling and silking when water demand peaks. Aphids and corn borers are a constant threat here, so I will spray three times. I am targeting 600 kg per mu.

For the 3.1 mu of cotton, I will plant a hybrid Bt cotton variety. Cotton pulls a lot of potassium out of the soil, so I will apply 22 kg nitrogen, 7 kg phosphorus, and 9 kg potassium per mu. I will rotary till that plot in early spring to warm the soil and break up the stubble. Cotton needs water at sowing, at flowering, and at the boll stage, so three irrigations. It also attracts every pest in the county despite the Bt trait, so I will spray five times. I expect 300 kg of seed cotton per mu.

I looked at what my neighbors are doing. The Wangs across the road are applying about the same rates, maybe 1 kg less nitrogen on wheat, but their plot is sandier and drains faster. My soil holds moisture better, so I stick to what my own fields have taught me. With fertilizer prices where they are — urea at about 120 yuan per 50 kg bag and compound fertilizer around 180 — this plan will cost me, but a bad harvest would cost far more. If I need extra hands at harvest, I will hire two workers for 120 yuan per day, but most of the year my wife and I can manage.
